mcclean-rockall.story: Rockall is a tiny bare rock in the North Atlantic, west of Scotland. Britain claimed it in 1955 and made it part of Scotland in 1972. Ireland has never claimed the rock itself but disputes Britain's position. Tom McClean, a Dublin-born adventurer who had served in Britain's Parachute Regiment and Special Air Service, went to live on it to strengthen Britain's claim, so his aim was the opposite of founding a breakaway state. He stayed from 26 May to 4 July 1985 in what one account calls a wooden box, a record 40 days alone. Whether people can live on Rockall matters because of the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the main treaty on ocean rights. Under it, a rock that cannot support human life or economic activity gets no exclusive economic zone (a belt of sea up to 200 nautical miles wide where a country controls fish and minerals) and no continental shelf (rights over the nearby seabed). Wikipedia's entry on McClean marks as doubtful the statement that his stay reaffirmed Britain's claim. Greenpeace activists passed his total in 1997 with 42 days, and Nick Hancock reached 45 days alone in 2014. Britain still claims the rock and 12 nautical miles of sea around it, and Ireland still disputes this.
mcclean-rockall.mechanism: Under the Law of the Sea treaty, a rock that cannot support human life earns no wide zone of sea or seabed rights. Living on one for 40 days was meant to support Britain's claim, but one person's stay does not settle that legal question.
mcclean-rockall.recognition: Not a claim of independence; meant to support Britain's claim

morac-songhrati-meads.story: The Republic of Morac-Songhrati-Meads was a paper claim to the Spratly Islands, a group of reefs and islets in the South China Sea that several countries dispute. Its supporters said a British sea captain, James George Meads, had claimed the islands in 1877 and called himself King James I, and that a rival branch of the family formed a Kingdom of Humanity in 1914. None of this has been shown to be true. The first evidence that can be checked comes from 1946, when Morton F. Meads, the captain's supposed descendant and an American soldier, was discharged in Manila over illegal private business, mainly reselling army surplus. Philippine newspapers printed his stories about a family birthright. Those stories drew the attention of Filipino businessmen such as Tomás Cloma, who then raced to claim the islands for the Philippines. The group never set up a settlement, and its activity was limited to items such as postage stamps. Meads asked the United Nations, the Republic of China and the Philippines for recognition in 1972 and got nowhere. According to the same account, the rest of its governing body drowned that year when Typhoon Ora sank their ship. In 1985 he sued the United States and others for $25 billion, and the case was never heard. His descendants were still making the claim in the 1990s.
morac-songhrati-meads.mechanism: A family claim with no documents and no one living on the land carried no legal weight. It reportedly mattered only because it pushed a rival private claimant into action, and that claim later fed into a country's argument for sovereignty, meaning its right to rule the islands.
morac-songhrati-meads.stopped_by: Ignored by the states that claim the islands
morac-songhrati-meads.challenge: Never tested in court; a 1985 lawsuit for $25 billion was not heard
morac-songhrati-meads.recognition: None; petitions to the United Nations, Republic of China and Philippines in 1972 failed
morac-songhrati-meads.why: Morton Meads's discharge was for illegal business ventures according to the listed page, where the old text said only private business.

principality-of-trinidad.story: Trindade is a small uninhabited island in the South Atlantic, off the coast of Brazil. James Harden-Hickey, a French-American writer and duellist, saw it on a voyage and treated it as terra nullius, a legal term for land that belongs to no one. In 1893 he proclaimed himself James I, Prince of Trinidad. He designed stamps, a flag and a coat of arms, founded a knightly order, bought a schooner to carry colonists and opened a consular office in New York. He also sold bonds to pay for building on the island. In 1895 The New York Times reported that the British warship Barracouta had taken possession of the island while he was in California. Britain wanted it as a station for a telegraph cable and based its claim on a visit by the astronomer Edmund Halley in 1700. Harden-Hickey appealed to the United States government without result. Brazil pressed its own claim, based on Portuguese discovery in 1502, and won the dispute with Britain. The Brazilian state of Espírito Santo put up a marker in January 1897, and Harden-Hickey died in El Paso, Texas, in February 1898. Trindade remains Brazilian, and the Brazilian navy keeps a post there.
principality-of-trinidad.mechanism: Claiming land as terra nullius, meaning owned by no one, only works while no country objects. Once Britain and Brazil took an interest, the question was settled between those governments by their old claims of discovery.
principality-of-trinidad.stopped_by: British landing in 1895, then Brazilian diplomacy
principality-of-trinidad.laws: He planned a military dictatorship and created a knightly order
principality-of-trinidad.challenge: Britain occupied the island in 1895, and Brazil's claim prevailed
principality-of-trinidad.cost: Government bonds were sold; the amount is unknown

waveland-rockall.story: The Global State of Waveland was a protest state declared by the environmental group Greenpeace on Rockall, a small rock in the North Atlantic about 301 kilometres from the nearest land in Scotland. Britain claimed the rock in 1955 and made it part of Scotland in 1972. Ireland, Iceland and Denmark have contested the rights around it, because whoever holds it might claim the surrounding seabed, where there may be oil. In June 1997 activists landed to protest oil exploration in the Atlantic, including a £1 billion field run by the oil company BP. They stayed 42 days, a record at the time. They declared the rock the capital of Waveland and offered citizenship to anyone who would take a pledge of allegiance. The Flags of the World website says Prime Minister Tony Blair refused their petition for recognition. The British government answered that Rockall was British territory and that anyone was free to go there and stay as long as they pleased. John Vidal, one of those who landed, said the team unscrewed the 1955 British plaque and refixed it back to front. Greenpeace used the occupation as a base for actions against rigs and ships surveying for oil, and landed again in 1998. Waveland has no standing in any country's law, and Britain still holds Rockall.
waveland-rockall.mechanism: Greenpeace used a disputed rock to draw attention to oil drilling. Because Britain treated the occupiers as ordinary visitors on British soil, it never had to act against their claim.
waveland-rockall.recognition: None; a petition to Britain for recognition was refused
waveland-rockall.challenge: No force was used; Britain said anyone could go there and stay

kiribati-floating-islands.story: Kiribati is a nation of low-lying islands in the central Pacific Ocean, threatened by rising seas. In September 2011, at a meeting of Pacific leaders in New Zealand, President Anote Tong told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation that his government was considering everything, including floating islands, because it was running out of options. He compared the idea to oil drilling rigs and asked what any person would do if the choice was to be submerged with their family or to climb onto a rig. He put the cost at about $2 billion, which would have to come from other countries. He named no site and showed no design. Three years later his government bought land in Fiji, another Pacific country. No platform was ever built. Under Article 60(8) of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the main treaty on ocean rights, an artificial island has no territorial sea of its own, meaning the band of coastal water a country fully controls.
kiribati-floating-islands.mechanism: A country can plan to move its people onto platforms, but the Law of the Sea treaty says artificial islands are not real islands. A platform would not by itself carry the sea rights that a country's land generates.
kiribati-floating-islands.recognition: A proposal made by a sitting head of state
kiribati-floating-islands.cost: About $2 billion, to come from other countries

xlii-seastead-phuket.story: XLII was a small floating home placed in the Andaman Sea about 14 nautical miles off Phuket, Thailand. A seastead is a permanent home at sea, and its backers hope to live under no country's laws. This one was a six-metre-wide cabin raised on a weighted column, paid for and built by a company called Ocean Builders. Chad Elwartowski, a 46-year-old American bitcoin trader, and his Thai partner Supranee Thepdet moved in during early 2019. Elwartowski said 20 more would be sold to form a community. The Thai navy said they had announced autonomy beyond the reach of any court and invited others to join, and Thailand treated this as an attack on its sovereignty, its right to rule its own territory. The couple left before the navy raided the cabin on 13 April 2019. Thailand revoked Elwartowski's visa and charged the two under a law that carries life in prison or death. On 22 April navy boats began towing the cabin to shore as evidence. Ocean Builders said it sat in the contiguous zone, the band 12 to 24 miles out where a country has only limited powers, and that no micronation was intended. Thailand pointed to its 200-mile exclusive economic zone, where a coastal state controls resources. In June 2019 officials said there had been no progress in arresting the couple, who had been traced to Tarutao island in April. In July prosecutors said nine more suspects would be charged. No report says how the case ended.
xlii-seastead-phuket.mechanism: Beyond 12 miles from shore a coastal country has limited powers, mainly over resources and customs. This case shows a country using its criminal law anyway, treating a private home in those waters as a threat to national security.
xlii-seastead-phuket.pop: Two people for about two months
xlii-seastead-phuket.laws: Occupants announced autonomy beyond any country's courts
xlii-seastead-phuket.challenge: Raided and towed away; occupants charged under a law carrying death or life in prison

add_sources.t: Phuket seasteading case stumbles along as Chad and Nadia get married, The Phuket News

central-tibetan-administration.story: The Central Tibetan Administration is the Tibetan government in exile, based in Dharamshala in northern India. Its roots lie in China's control of Tibet. In March 1959, as he fled to India, the 14th Dalai Lama, Tibet's religious leader and then its head of government, rejected the 1951 Seventeen Point Agreement with China. He re-established his cabinet, the Kashag, in exile that April. The administration now has courts, a parliament and an executive, under a charter adopted in 1991. In 2011 the Dalai Lama gave up his political duties, and executive power passed to an elected leader called the Sikyong. Penpa Tsering was sworn in for a second five-year term in May 2026. Tibetans abroad vote for the parliament and the Sikyong and make yearly contributions recorded in the Green Book, a document sometimes called a passport. Money comes mainly from private donations, these contributions and aid from governments such as India and the United States. No country recognises the administration as a sovereign government, meaning one with the legal right to rule Tibet, although it receives aid for welfare work. It operates from India and continues to run elections.
central-tibetan-administration.mechanism: A government in exile can hold elections and collect contributions from its people with no territory of its own. Without recognition from other countries, it has no legal standing as a state.
central-tibetan-administration.passports: Green Book, a record of contributions also called a passport

rada-of-belarusian-republic.story: The Rada of the Belarusian Democratic Republic, also known as the Belarusian People's Republic, is a council that has claimed to represent Belarus from exile for more than a century. It began in Minsk in 1918, during the First World War, when German forces occupied the area. On 25 March 1918 it declared independence and asked Germany for support, but Germany did not officially recognise it, although the Rada had diplomatic contacts with neighbours such as Finland, the Ukrainian People's Republic and the Baltic states. When Bolshevik armies advanced at the end of 1918 it left Minsk, moving through Grodno and Vilnius to Kaunas, and it has been in exile since 1919. A Red Army advance in 1945 forced it to move again, to western Germany. Today it works as an advocacy group among Belarusians in North America, Britain and elsewhere, pressing Western officials to support Belarusian independence and democracy. Ivonka Survilla has been its president since 1997. It says it holds a symbolic mandate that it wants to hand to a democratically elected Belarusian parliament. It supported the opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya during the 2020–2021 protests, and the Belarusian KGB declared it an extremist group in June 2023. It holds no territory and calls itself the oldest existing government in exile.
rada-of-belarusian-republic.mechanism: A government in exile can survive for more than a century as an organisation of people abroad, holding no land and acting only as a voice for its cause.
rada-of-belarusian-republic.recognition: Germany did not recognise it in 1918; today it claims only a symbolic mandate
rada-of-belarusian-republic.why: Recognition field held research narration; replaced with what the page states about 1918 and its symbolic mandate. Added 1945 move and 2023 extremist designation.

a23a-iceberg.story: A23a was the largest iceberg in the world for much of its life, and it carried away part of a Soviet research base. It broke from the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf, a floating sheet of ice attached to Antarctica, in 1986. The Soviet base Druzhnaya I stood on that part of the shelf, so the base went with it, and a rescue mission began in 1987 to move what could be saved. Rusted debris from the base could still be seen in the edge of the ice in January 2025. The iceberg sat stuck on the sea bed for many years and began moving in 2020. In January 2025 it measured about 3,500 square kilometres. It spun over an undersea mountain through much of 2024, then grounded 73 kilometres from the island of South Georgia in March 2025 and floated off again by July. By September 2025 it was breaking up in warmer water, and in March 2026 it was down to 180 square kilometres. Monitoring then stopped, and by July 2026 it was thought to be gone or nearly so.
a23a-iceberg.mechanism: Anything built on an ice shelf can drift away with it when the ice breaks off, leaving the fixed place it was built on. Even an iceberg of this size lasted only about 40 years, so floating ice offers no lasting ground for a settlement.
a23a-iceberg.stopped_by: Melting and break-up in warmer water

camp-barneo.story: Camp Barneo was a private tourist camp built each spring on floating sea ice in the Arctic Ocean near the North Pole, in waters beyond any country's land. The Russian Alexander Orlov founded it in 2002. His widow Irina Orlova ran it after him, then sold it to the Swedish billionaire Frederik Paulsen. Because the ice keeps moving, the camp had to be rebuilt from nothing each April, and in 2007 winds pushed it southeast at 0.8 kilometres an hour. A visit cost about $20,000. From 2002 to 2017 every trip started and ended at Longyearbyen on Svalbard, a Norwegian archipelago, so the camp relied on Norway for its flights. In 2016, after Chechen paratroopers held military exercises at Barneo, Norway imposed a flight ban, which it later lifted. A dispute between Russia and Ukraine stopped tourist flights in 2019, and COVID-19 cancelled the 2020 and 2021 seasons. Plans for 2022 ended with Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and a 2024 season meant to leave from Russia was also cancelled. The camp last operated in 2018.
camp-barneo.mechanism: A camp on drifting ice may sit beyond any country, but it still needs an airport. The country that controls the airport can shut the camp down by limiting flights.
camp-barneo.stopped_by: Norwegian flight limits, the Russia-Ukraine dispute, COVID-19 and the 2022 invasion of Ukraine
camp-barneo.recognition: None; run under the patronage of the Russian Geographical Society

north-pole-drift-stations.story: The North Pole stations are research camps that the Soviet Union, and later Russia, has placed on floating Arctic sea ice to study the ocean and weather. On 21 May 1937 the Soviet Union set up North Pole-1 on an ice floe about 20 kilometres from the Pole, in an expedition led by Otto Schmidt. Four men lived there for nine months while the floe drifted 2,850 kilometres, until icebreaker ships took them off in February 1938. They came home as Heroes of the Soviet Union. From 1954, one to three stations ran each year. A typical camp began in April and lasted two or three years, until its floe reached the Greenland Sea, and North Pole-22 drifted for nine years. The program stopped after the Soviet Union ended and resumed in 2003. From the mid-2000s it became hard to find a safe floe, and several stations were evacuated early because the ice melted too fast. Russia therefore ordered a self-propelled, ice-resistant platform called North Pole in 2017, to replace camps on bare ice. It was completed in August 2022, ran station NP-41 from 2022 to 2024 and started NP-42 in 2024. All the stations have been run by one government body, the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute.
north-pole-drift-stations.mechanism: People can live on drifting sea ice for years if a government supplies them. These stations stayed state property throughout, and thinning ice has now led Russia to put its station on a vessel.
north-pole-drift-stations.pop: About 800 people across all stations since 1937, replaced each year

project-habakkuk.story: Project Habakkuk was a British plan during the Second World War to build a giant aircraft carrier out of ice. Geoffrey Pyke, who worked for Britain's Combined Operations command, proposed levelling an iceberg, natural or artificial, into an airbase in the middle of the Atlantic, out of the range of planes flying from land. The scientist Max Perutz warned in 1942 that real icebergs have too little surface above water and can roll over. The idea survived because of pykrete, a frozen mix of water and wood pulp that was stronger than ice and slower to melt. The plan then became a ship 600 metres long. Pykrete still sagged slowly unless kept at minus 16 degrees Celsius, so the vessel would have needed insulation and refrigeration. A prototype 18 metres by 9 metres, weighing 1,000 tons, was built on Patricia Lake in Alberta, Canada. As the work went on, the estimated cost grew from £700,000 to £2.5 million, and Canada said it could not be done that season. The project's board last met in December 1943 and called the large ship impractical, so it was never built.
project-habakkuk.mechanism: The largest ice platform ever seriously planned needed constant refrigeration and a government budget. It would have been a warship under Britain's flag with no separate legal status.
project-habakkuk.stopped_by: Project board, December 1943, on cost and technical grounds

uae-iceberg-project.story: This was a plan to tow a large iceberg from the Southern Ocean to the United Arab Emirates, a desert country on the Persian Gulf, for its fresh water. Abdulla Alsheni, an Emirati businessman who owned National Adviser Bureau Limited, announced it in 2017. The iceberg would come from the area of Heard Island to the coast of Fujairah and might yield 20 billion gallons of water. The idea was older. In 1977 Saudi Arabia's Prince Mohammad al Faisal set up a company, Iceberg Transport International, for the same purpose, and that plan was never carried out. Alsheni presented his project to two UAE ministries, with a trial planned for early 2022 and a final tow in late 2023, at a cost of $100 to 150 million. The project's website claimed that under the freedom of the high seas, the rule that open ocean belongs to no country, anyone may take icebergs for private use. In a 2022 article in the journal Ius Novum, the legal writer Mateusz Osiecki tested that claim. He concluded that a free-floating iceberg is probably no state's property, noted that writers hold three different views, and set out the duties under the 1991 Environmental Protocol to the Antarctic Treaty. He also noted that the UAE belongs to neither the Antarctic Treaty system nor the Law of the Sea treaty. No report says that a tow took place.
uae-iceberg-project.mechanism: No treaty names the owner of a floating iceberg. A private tow would rely on the freedom of the high seas, the rule that open ocean belongs to no country, and no court has tested that argument.
uae-iceberg-project.founder: Abdulla Alsheni, National Adviser Bureau Limited
uae-iceberg-project.recognition: None sought; the legal position is untested

bogota-declaration.story: The Bogotá Declaration was a claim by eight countries on the equator to part of outer space. They signed it on 3 December 1976 at the end of a meeting in Bogotá, Colombia. The signers were Ecuador, Colombia, Brazil, Congo, Zaire, Uganda, Kenya and Indonesia. Their target was geostationary orbit, the ring about 36,000 kilometres above the equator where a satellite seems to stay fixed over one spot, which makes it valuable for communications. The declaration called this orbit a scarce natural resource and said the part above each signer's territory fell under that country's sovereignty, meaning its full legal control. Parts over the open ocean were to be the common heritage of mankind, run by all nations together. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans national claims in space, so the signers argued that the treaty had never defined where outer space begins and therefore did not cover the orbit above their land. Many were newly independent and resented a rule set by countries that already had satellites. The claim won little support elsewhere, but two signers kept it in their law. Article 101 of Colombia's constitution lists its segment of the orbit as part of the country, and Colombia's Constitutional Court said in 2004 that the country had not given up sovereignty over it. Article 4 of Ecuador's 2008 constitution also asserts rights over the orbit. Other countries have not accepted the claim.
bogota-declaration.mechanism: The Outer Space Treaty bans countries from claiming space but never says where space begins. Equatorial countries tried to use that silence to claim the orbit above them, and other countries' refusal left the treaty's ban in place.
bogota-declaration.stopped_by: Lack of international support; Colombia and Ecuador still assert the claim in their constitutions

tongasat.story: Tongasat is a company that files for and rents out satellite positions on behalf of Tonga, a small kingdom in the South Pacific. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a United Nations agency, assigns places in geostationary orbit, the ring above the equator where a satellite stays over one spot, to countries that apply. In 1987 Matt Nilson, a businessman who had moved to Tonga from San Diego, persuaded the king, through Princess Pilolevu, that even a tiny country could apply. The government authorised the venture in April 1988, and in March 1990 Nilson applied for 16 of the 180 slots then available. Intelsat, a satellite operator, and the United States objected. The ITU agreed in March 1991 after he cut the request to six, and Tonga eventually held nine. The plan was to rent each slot for $2 million a year, with half the profit going to the government. A company called Rimsat rented slots in 1992, and Nilson was fired in February 1994 after an audit found he owned Rimsat shares. China later wanted the slot at 130 degrees East, and Tonga gave way in exchange for grant aid, part of which went to Tongasat. On 17 August 2018 Lord Chief Justice Paulsen ruled that the company had unlawfully received over $46 million in public money. In 2019 the court refused Tongasat's request to bring new evidence to its appeal and ordered it to pay about $15,000 as security for costs by 1 November, or the appeal would be put on hold. No report says how the appeal finally ended.
tongasat.mechanism: ITU rules let any country, however small, apply for satellite positions and then rent them to foreign operators. That turned a country's right to apply into something that could be sold.
tongasat.founder: Matt Nilson, with Princess Salote Pilolevu Tuita and King Taufa'ahau Tupou IV
tongasat.stopped_by: Tonga's Supreme Court ruled against the company over Chinese grant money in 2018
tongasat.laws: Agency agreement with the Kingdom of Tonga; filings with the ITU
tongasat.challenge: Lost in Tonga's Supreme Court over more than $46 million in public money
tongasat.recognition: The ITU accepted its filings; many operators and governments objected
tongasat.cost: Slots rented at $2 million a year each; over $46 million in Chinese grant aid went to the company
tongasat.why: Named Nilson as Matt Nilson per the listed Wikipedia page.

aisland-landi.story: Aisland was a large flat barge anchored about 30 miles off Dubai in the Persian Gulf, where an Italian businessman lived while planning his own country at sea. Samuele Landi's company, Eutelia, went bankrupt in 2010. He was tried for fraud in Italy and sentenced in his absence to 14 years, and he moved to Dubai. The reporter Ian Urbina of the Outlaw Ocean Project writes that Landi avoided extradition, the handing over of a suspect to another country, and obtained diplomatic credentials from Liberia. Landi bought the 800-ton barge and bolted six shipping containers to the deck as living quarters, with solar air conditioning and a machine to make fresh water from seawater. He lived aboard for over a year with three sailors, a cook and five cats, raising money for a larger barge to take to the Saya de Malha Bank, a huge underwater plateau in the Indian Ocean, most of it in international waters. He hoped for about twenty barges and thousands of residents by 2028, and planned to mount a Gatling gun against pirates. The Seasteading Institute says a captain warned him the barge was unsafe. On 2 February 2024 a wave broke it in two. Two crew members survived by clinging to wood until a passing ship picked them up the next day. Landi and two employees, named as Abdul and Javed Khan, died, and his body came ashore about 40 miles up the coast. The project ended with his death.
aisland-landi.mechanism: Landi hoped distance from land would keep him beyond extradition. Living at sea also meant no authority was shown to be checking the barge's safety, since no account names a flag state (the country whose rules a vessel sails under) or an inspection body.
aisland-landi.stopped_by: A wave broke the barge on 2 February 2024; three people died
aisland-landi.pop: Landi and a small crew: three sailors and a cook, by one account
aisland-landi.cost: Planned about twenty barges by 2028; cost unknown

bakov-arca-noe.story: This is a Russian businessman's project to restore the Russian Empire as a small state somewhere outside Russia. Anton Bakov, a former member of Russia's parliament who chairs the Monarchist Party, founded it in 2011. Under the name Imperial Throne it issued a manifesto on 31 March 2014 naming a German prince, Karl Emich of Leiningen, as Emperor Nicholas III, with Bakov as prime minister and later Archchancellor. It took the name Romanov Empire in 2017. It sold passports online for 1,000 rubles, about 31 American dollars, and claimed about 4,000 by 2014. In 2013 it said it had given citizenship to Edward Snowden, the American who leaked secret surveillance files. Because a state needs land and it had none, its leaders looked for some. Nicholas III asked Vladimir Putin for land in Yekaterinburg and was refused, and Bakov's talks to buy territory from Kiribati and the Gambia had failed by 2017. In 2020 Bakov announced a successor project called Arca Noë, to be based in what he called neutral Mediterranean waters close to Venice, as part of the seasteading movement, which aims to build permanent homes at sea. No structure has been reported.
bakov-arca-noe.mechanism: After several governments refused to sell or give land, the project moved its claim to open water, where no state's consent seemed necessary. Holding no land, it stayed a claim with passports and nothing built.
bakov-arca-noe.stopped_by: Kiribati, the Gambia and Russia did not provide land
bakov-arca-noe.passports: Sold online for 1,000 rubles; about 4,000 claimed by 2014

oceania-atlantis-project.story: The Atlantis Project was a plan to build a new country called Oceania on platforms in the Caribbean Sea off Panama. Eric Klien started it in February 1993, after he said election fraud had cost a Libertarian candidate, Tamara Clark, a Nevada state senate race. He wanted a place to start government over. Oceania was to begin as about 80 hexagon-shaped units holding 10,000 to 30,000 people. The project's own online guide priced the start at roughly one billion dollars and placed the site about fifty miles northeast of Panama, on water it described as 100 feet deep, near trade routes, in an area it said had no recorded hurricanes. It published a full constitution and legal code before anything was built, under the slogan "Break the Chains". Promotion ran largely through mailing lists and an online discussion group. Klien later told VICE that the main reason it failed was too little interest, and that reaching people before the web was costly, through phones and newspaper advertisements. The project's guide says it collapsed in April 1994. Klien went on to run the Lifeboat Foundation. A site 50 miles off Panama would have sat inside the exclusive economic zone, the 200-mile belt where the Law of the Sea treaty gives a coastal country control of resources, but nothing was built, so the question never came up.
oceania-atlantis-project.mechanism: Oceania counted on being outside the 12-mile limit of a country's full control. Its site still lay within Panama's 200-mile resource zone, a conflict that was never tested because nothing was built.
oceania-atlantis-project.laws: A complete constitution and legal code were written in advance

seasteading-institute.story: The Seasteading Institute is an American non-profit that promotes seasteads, permanent homes at sea. Wayne Gramlich and Patri Friedman founded it on 15 April 2008 because they wanted room to try new forms of government. They pointed out that under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a country's exclusive economic zone, where it controls resources, runs 200 nautical miles from shore, and beyond it the high seas fall under no country's law apart from that of a ship's flag state, the country it is registered in. Peter Thiel, a co-founder of PayPal, gave $500,000. The founders hoped to float a prototype in San Francisco Bay by 2010 and a seastead by 2014, and they met neither target. In January 2009 the institute patented ClubStead, a design for a 200-person resort about the size of a city block. In July 2009 Friedman launched Ephemerisle, a floating gathering in the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta inside California, which continued without him. The institute later turned to working inside a country's waters. On 13 January 2017 it signed a memorandum of understanding, a non-binding agreement, with French Polynesia for a floating island prototype with partial self-rule. After political changes linked to a presidential election, the government pulled out and cut ties on 14 March 2018. No one lives on an institute seastead. It was still publishing in 2024, promoting safety standards after the death of Samuele Landi.
seasteading-institute.mechanism: The institute's starting idea is that the high seas beyond 200 miles offer a place to try new forms of government, subject only to a flag state. Its one real deal instead sought a government's permission, and that government withdrew it.
seasteading-institute.pop: No one lives on an institute seastead
seasteading-institute.cost: Peter Thiel gave $500,000 in early funding

akon-city.story: Akon City was a planned futuristic city on the coast of Senegal in West Africa, promoted by the singer Akon, who was born in the United States and partly raised in Senegal. He announced it in June 2018 at the Cannes Lions advertising festival, saying it would run on his own cryptocurrency, Akoin, and that President Macky Sall had given him 2,000 acres, about 800 hectares. On 13 January 2020 he signed a memorandum of understanding, a preliminary agreement, with Sapco, Senegal's state tourism development body, in the presence of the tourism minister. A groundbreaking ceremony followed in August 2020. The reported cost was $6 billion, to come mainly from American private partners, with a first phase by 2023 and completion by 2029. Commentators compared the curving tower designs with Wakanda from the Black Panther films. The city did not appear on schedule. In 2025 the head of Sapco, Serigne Mamadou Mboup, told the BBC that the Akon City project no longer exists. He said Akon and Sapco had agreed on a more realistic project that Sapco would support.
akon-city.mechanism: A special city still depends on a state agency for its land. The agency can take that land back or change the deal if nothing gets built.
akon-city.stopped_by: Sapco, Senegal's state tourism body, said in 2025 that the project no longer exists
akon-city.challenge: Cancelled by the state agency that controlled the land deal
akon-city.recognition: Backed by Senegal's government at first

bitcoin-city.story: Bitcoin City is a planned city in La Unión, El Salvador, at the foot of the Conchagua volcano. President Nayib Bukele announced it in November 2021, after his country had adopted the digital currency bitcoin. Geothermal power from the volcano was to be used to mine bitcoin, the computer process that creates new coins. The city was to be circular, like a coin, and almost free of taxes apart from a 13 percent value-added tax, a sales tax, half of which would pay off bonds. Money was to come from a $1 billion "volcano bond" involving the state power company LaGeo, with half for the city and half for buying bitcoin. Some bond buyers might receive Salvadoran citizenship. NBC reported that analysts paid more attention to the bonds than to the city. Delays in financing and construction followed. Under a later deal with the International Monetary Fund, a global lender to governments in financial trouble, businesses no longer had to accept bitcoin and taxes could no longer be paid in it. The Week described this as ending bitcoin's run as effective legal tender, meaning money everyone must accept. An airport in the plan was expected to start operating in 2027, according to a 2025 source. No report describes the city itself as built.
bitcoin-city.mechanism: A government can promise a low-tax zone by decree, but it still needs lenders and bond buyers to pay for it. Those lenders can attach conditions that undo the plan.
bitcoin-city.laws: Almost no taxes planned, apart from a 13 percent value-added tax
bitcoin-city.challenge: Undercut by an International Monetary Fund deal limiting the bitcoin policy
bitcoin-city.cost: A planned $1 billion volcano bond, half for the city and half to buy bitcoin

cheran.story: Cherán is a town of the Indigenous Purépecha people in the state of Michoacán, Mexico, that threw out the police and politicians and now governs itself. For more than three years, armed loggers and masked men demanding money had worked there without being punished, and by 2011 the loggers were close to one of the town's water springs. A group of local women met in secret and decided to stop the trucks in town, where neighbours could back them up. The uprising drove out the loggers, the police and the politicians. Political parties were banned, and they were still banned when the BBC visited five years later. Each of the four districts elected representatives to a ruling council. Armed checkpoints went up on the three main roads, staffed by the Ronda Comunitaria, a local force of men and women who stop every vehicle and question those inside. The community also asked to choose its authorities by its own customs. On 2 November 2011 Mexico's federal Electoral Tribunal ordered Michoacán's electoral authority and state congress to act on that request. The town is now described as a self-ruling Indigenous community largely free of the crime and corruption that caused the revolt. It does not claim to be a separate country.
cheran.mechanism: An Indigenous community can replace state police and party politics inside its own boundaries while staying part of the country. In Cherán's case the federal election court backed its right to choose leaders by custom.
cheran.founder: Women of Cherán, a Purépecha town
cheran.challenge: Survived; treated as a self-ruling Indigenous community
cheran.recognition: A 2011 federal Electoral Tribunal ruling backed its request to elect leaders by custom

difc.story: The Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) is a 110-hectare business district in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, with its own commercial law and courts. In September 2004 a federal law allowed each emirate to set up legal structures for financial centres. Dubai Law No. 9 of 2004 then created the centre, and Dubai Law No. 12 created its courts, which began working in 2006. Inside the zone, civil and commercial cases follow common law, the English system built on past court rulings, in English, separately from the rest of the country's legal system. It has its own financial regulator and offers companies a 50-year guarantee of zero tax on corporate income. Other laws, such as criminal law and immigration rules, still apply there. At first the courts could hear only cases tied to the zone. A law of 31 October 2011 let them hear any local or international commercial case if all parties agree, so firms with no link to the zone can also use them. The zone remains part of Dubai.
difc.mechanism: A country can set aside its own commercial law inside a defined zone without giving up any sovereignty, because the zone's powers come from the country's own statutes and can be changed by them. Criminal law still applies inside.
difc.laws: English-language common-law courts for business cases; own financial regulator; national criminal law still applies
difc.recognition: Created and backed by federal and Dubai law

forest-city.story: Forest City is a $100 billion housing project on the coast of Johor, Malaysia, about a 30-minute drive from Singapore. The Chinese developer Country Garden started it in 2016 and marketed it mainly to buyers in mainland China as a luxury home for 700,000 people. Country Garden told Bloomberg that 9,000 people lived there, while the magazine Domus reported in July 2024 that just over 1 percent of the development was thought to be inhabited. Business Insider reported that the company owed over $190 billion. To revive the area, Malaysia launched a Special Financial Zone covering it on 20 September 2024, with tax breaks from early 2025. They included a zero rate for family offices, private firms that manage the wealth of rich families, and lower personal income tax for some people who move there. Analysts quoted by BenarNews disagreed on whether this would work. The project never sought sovereignty, and it stays under Malaysian law with a state-backed tax arrangement.
forest-city.mechanism: A country can create a special tax zone to rescue a private development. The tax breaks come from the state, so its authority over the area does not change.
forest-city.laws: Malaysian law, with Special Financial Zone tax rules from 2025
forest-city.challenge: The developer's debts undermine it; no one has challenged sovereignty
forest-city.recognition: The Malaysian government sponsors the zone

freetown-christiania.story: Freetown Christiania is a self-governing community of about 900 people on the site of an old military barracks in the Christianshavn district of Copenhagen, Denmark. Squatters moved in during 1971 and set up a community with free cannabis, little government, no cars and no police. An article in a local paper proclaimed a free town. The Defence Ministry sued in 1976, and the Supreme Court ruled on 2 February 1978 that the site should be cleared at once, but this was never carried out. Later governments tried to close it, often over the open sale of hashish. After hard talks, residents agreed in June 2011 to set up a fund to buy the land. With the first payment in July 2012 they became legal owners of part of it, and the rest stayed with the state. A foundation now runs the area. After repeated shootings, residents and authorities dug up the main dealing lane, Pusher Street, on 6 April 2024, which unlocked state money for renovation and for joining the area to the wider city. In February 2026 residents reluctantly accepted a public housing plan for about 300 people, with building possibly starting around 2029. Christiania draws half a million visitors a year and remains under Danish law.
freetown-christiania.mechanism: Some forty years of official tolerance, followed by buying the land, gave a squat secure legal title inside the state. It stayed fully under Danish law.
freetown-christiania.laws: Residents' meetings and working groups; a foundation holds the land
freetown-christiania.recognition: The Danish state negotiated with it; no state recognises it as independent
freetown-christiania.cost: Residents set up a fund in 2011 to buy the land; first payment July 2012
freetown-christiania.why: Legal point said fifty years of tolerance before purchase; 1971 to 2012 is about forty.

add_sources.t: Christiania locals fear newcomers could threaten area's hippie soul, The Local

maldives-floating-city.story: Maldives Floating City is a planned housing project on a 200-hectare lagoon about 10 minutes by boat from Malé, the capital of the Maldives, a low-lying island nation in the Indian Ocean. It is promoted as an answer to rising seas, since homes that float would rise with the water. The government signed it with the Dutch developer Dutch Docklands in 2010. It stalled after a change of government in February 2012 and was signed again on 8 May 2019, when five lagoons were allotted to the company. The deal was revised on 23 June 2022. A ministry reply reported by Atoll Times said no work had begun on the lagoons, none had been reclaimed and two had been sold, and Economy Minister Fayyaz Ismail called the project a scam. In June 2023 the company said the plan had changed at the government's request, with first prices lowered to about $100,000, work starting that August and completion in early 2028. Reports differ on progress. One said no mockup had been shown despite three announced dates, and a February 2023 report said a mockup could be seen in the Hulhumalé lagoon. In May 2024 Newsweek published satellite images it described as showing construction, and lead architect Koen Olthuis expected first residents within 14 months. Other accounts give about 5,000 units for 20,000 residents, opening in 2027. No later report confirms finished homes or residents.
maldives-floating-city.mechanism: The project rests on lagoon leases from the Maldives government, so it would stay wholly Maldivian. Floating gives it no separate legal standing.

mount-athos.story: Mount Athos is a 335-square-kilometre mountainous peninsula in northern Greece, home to 20 Orthodox Christian monasteries, that governs itself under Greek law. Monks have lived there since at least the 9th century. Most of the peninsula is run as a self-governing region of Greece by the monks themselves, and in church matters it answers to the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople, the senior bishop of Orthodox Christianity. A 10th-century charter bars female animals, and Greek law and religious tradition exclude women, who may not come within 500 metres of the coast. Dr Graham Speake, an author on Athos, told the BBC that the charter did not mention women because everyone already knew they were not allowed in men's monasteries. Tradition also holds that the Virgin Mary was blown off course and landed there, and that the mountain was set aside for her alone. Because the monks control entry, visitors need a special permit. A man sends a copy of his passport to the Pilgrims' Bureau, and each day 100 Orthodox and 10 non-Orthodox men are admitted for three nights. Vladimir Putin has visited to mark 1,000 years of Russian monks there. UNESCO, the United Nations cultural agency, listed the site in 1988. It remains part of Greece with this special status.
mount-athos.mechanism: A religious community can keep real self-government, and even its own entry permit system, for more than a thousand years because the state's own law recognises it. Its self-rule depends on that recognition.
mount-athos.founder: Orthodox monks, present since at least the 9th century
mount-athos.pop: Monks of 20 monasteries; only men may enter
mount-athos.passports: Entry permit from the Pilgrims' Bureau
mount-athos.laws: Run by the monks under Greek law; in church matters, under the Ecumenical Patriarch
mount-athos.recognition: A self-governing region of Greece; UNESCO listed 1988

prospera-zede.story: Próspera is a private business zone with its own rules on Roatán, an island off the north coast of Honduras. In 2013 Honduras changed its constitution to allow Zones for Employment and Economic Development (ZEDEs), areas with their own laws, courts and taxes. An earlier plan called Special Development Regions had been struck down as a breach of sovereignty, the country's right to govern itself. Erick Brimen, a Venezuelan-born fund manager, applied in 2017 and built Próspera with American venture capital, through a Delaware company that holds a veto on its council. It offers single-digit taxes, its own regulations and a court of retired Arizona judges who hear cases online. Neighbours in the village of Crawfish Rock feared losing their land. President Xiomara Castro signed a repeal of the ZEDE law in April 2022, saying Honduras was recovering its sovereignty. On 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court declared the ZEDE laws unconstitutional, with retroactive effect. Próspera's owners had already claimed about $10.7 billion from Honduras at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID), a World Bank body that decides disputes between investors and governments. They relied on a promise of stable rules and on CAFTA-DR, a trade treaty between the United States and Central American countries. Honduras left ICSID in August 2024, then rejoined with effect from 16 August 2026. Honduran officials said in October 2025 that the claim had dropped to $1.63 billion. The case was still pending in October 2026, when the tribunal issued an order about a site visit, and the zone continues to operate during the dispute.
prospera-zede.mechanism: A country can hand lawmaking to a private zone and later take it back through its own courts. An investment treaty may still let the company sue for damages before an international tribunal.
prospera-zede.stopped_by: Honduras: 2022 repeal law and 2024 Supreme Court ruling; the zone keeps running during the dispute
prospera-zede.laws: Own regulations, single-digit taxes, private arbitration with retired Arizona judges
prospera-zede.challenge: Legal basis struck down on 20 September 2024; the company went to international arbitration, a private tribunal
prospera-zede.recognition: Granted by an earlier Honduran government; later revoked
prospera-zede.cost: ICSID claim originally about $10.8 billion, reduced to about $1.63 billion according to the Honduran attorney general
prospera-zede.why: Old text said a site visit took place in October 2026; ICSID lists only a procedural order on a site visit dated 22 October 2026.

sark.story: Sark is a 5.44-square-kilometre island in the Channel Islands, between England and France, with about 500 people and a form of government that stayed feudal into the 21st century. In 1565 Queen Elizabeth I granted it to Helier de Carteret, of Jersey, as a fief, land held from the Crown in return for service. His conditions were to clear out pirates and keep at least 40 loyal men there, so he rented out 40 plots called tenements. The island's parliament, Chief Pleas, long consisted of the Seigneur, or feudal lord, the Seneschal, a judge, the 40 tenement holders and 12 elected deputies. The billionaire brothers David and Frederick Barclay bought the neighbouring islet of Brecqhou in 1993. In the mid-1990s they went to the European Court of Human Rights to challenge Sark's inheritance law, which required their island to pass to David's eldest son. Women gained equal inheritance rights in 1999. The brothers then argued that the whole system broke the European Convention on Human Rights, and it was replaced under a new constitution in 2008. Candidates backed by their businesses won few seats in the elections of 2008 and 2010. Sark remains part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, a self-governing Crown Dependency, a territory that belongs to the British Crown but is not part of the United Kingdom.
sark.mechanism: Very old self-rule inside a larger legal system must still follow the human rights law that binds that system. Sark's feudal government had to change for that reason.
sark.laws: Own parliament (Chief Pleas); laws based on Norman law
sark.challenge: Feudal government was changed in 2008 after a human rights challenge
sark.recognition: Part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, a British Crown Dependency

vatican-lateran-treaty.story: Vatican City is the world's smallest state, a 44-hectare area inside Rome, created by a 1929 treaty between the Pope and Italy. Popes had ruled central Italy as the Papal States until Italian forces captured Rome in 1870. Italy's Law of Guarantees of 1871 offered the pope use of the Vatican and Lateran palaces and 3,250,000 lire a year, but no sovereignty, meaning no independent right to rule. The Holy See, the Pope's government, refused, and each pope after that called himself a prisoner in the Vatican. This dispute, called the Roman Question, stayed open for about 60 years. On 11 February 1929, at the Lateran Palace, the Holy See under Pius XI and Italy under King Victor Emmanuel III and Benito Mussolini signed the Lateran Pacts. The treaty recognised the Holy See's full sovereignty over the newly created State of Vatican City, and a financial agreement settled claims over lost land. Italy's 1948 constitution recognised the treaty, and a 1984 revision ended Catholicism's status as the sole state religion. Vatican City had 882 residents in 2024 and remains a sovereign state.
vatican-lateran-treaty.mechanism: A new sovereign state can be created by a treaty with the country around it. Its standing rests on that country's consent and on other governments accepting it.
vatican-lateran-treaty.laws: Rule by the Pope; the Holy See is itself a sovereign body
vatican-lateran-treaty.recognition: Recognised by Italy by treaty; treated as a sovereign state

haudenosaunee-passport.story: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy, also called the Iroquois, is an alliance of Indigenous nations in New York State and Canada that regards itself as sovereign and has issued its own passports since at least 1923. That year one went to the Cayuga statesman Deskaheh so he could travel to the League of Nations in Geneva. The modern form has been used since 1977. Other countries treat it unevenly. Japan admitted a delegation on it in 2005. In early 2010 a delegation from Kahnawake was stranded in El Salvador for weeks trying to return on it. In July 2010 Britain refused it for the Haudenosaunee lacrosse team travelling to the World Championship, and the United States offered the players American passports, which they rejected. Israel accepted the team's passports in July 2018, subject to Canadian assurances that they could return, and Ireland accepted them in August 2022. The European Union and the Isle of Man list it as a "fantasy passport", one issued by a body they do not treat as a state. The United States, British and Canadian governments have refused to endorse it, and it is not accepted for entry into Canada. It is still issued and still judged case by case.
haudenosaunee-passport.mechanism: A passport works only where other countries choose to honour it. For a nation without recognition as a state, that choice is made case by case.
haudenosaunee-passport.recognition: Accepted case by case by Japan, Israel and Ireland; rejected by the European Union

hawaiian-sovereignty-movement.story: The Hawaiian sovereignty movement is a collection of Native Hawaiian groups seeking self-government or an independent nation for Hawaii, now a state of the United States. Their case goes back to 1893, when a group mostly of Americans living in the kingdom overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani with the support of armed sailors from the warship USS Boston, and to the American annexation of 1898, which the movement regards as illegal. In 1993 Congress passed the Apology Resolution, acknowledging that the overthrow was illegal. The groups differ on what should follow. Ka Lāhui Hawaiʻi, started in 1987 with Mililani Trask as first governor, has a constitution and elected officers, and it reported 21,000 members in 1997. In 1993 it led 10,000 people on a march to Iolani Palace. The Nation of Hawaiʻi, led by Dennis "Bumpy" Kanahele, wants a republic. It occupied the area around Makapuʻu lighthouse in 1989 and Kaupo Beach in 1993, and it ended that occupation in exchange for land. The Akaka Bill, proposed in 2000, would have begun federal recognition of a Native Hawaiian government, much like that given to Native American tribes. Many sovereignty groups opposed it, and a 2005 Grassroot Institute poll found most Hawaii residents opposed it too. In 2015 the Interior Department announced a procedure for recognising a Native Hawaiian government, and Justice Anthony Kennedy halted the counting of votes for a planned convention that November. Hawaii remains a state, and the groups remain divided on their goals.
hawaiian-sovereignty-movement.mechanism: A government's apology for an illegal act does not by itself restore sovereignty or return land. Any change would need new law or a new negotiation.
hawaiian-sovereignty-movement.laws: United States and Hawaii law apply

kingitanga.story: The Kīngitanga, or Māori King Movement, is a line of Māori monarchs in New Zealand that began as a rival authority to British colonial rule. In the 1850s chiefs in the central North Island wanted unity to slow European land purchases and a monarch of equal standing to Queen Victoria. Pōtatau Te Wherowhero was crowned at Ngāruawāhia in June 1858. In 1861 Wiremu Tamihana, the chief known as the kingmaker, wrote that Māori were a separate nation, and the colonial government saw the movement as a challenge to the British monarchy. Governor Grey issued an ultimatum on 9 July 1863, and troops crossed into the Waikato region three days later. The government confiscated 486,500 hectares from those it called rebels, including farmed land and burial sites. After defeats including Ōrākau in 1864, King Tāwhiao and his followers withdrew into the land of the Ngāti Maniapoto tribe, later called the King Country, and declared that Europeans crossing its boundary, the aukati, risked death. In 1881 Tāwhiao and 70 followers laid down their guns at Alexandra and declared peace. The movement continues, centred on the Waikato-Tainui tribes, although New Zealand law and many tribes do not recognise the monarch. Nga wai hono i te po became its eighth monarch in September 2024. In 2014 the Waitangi Tribunal, which hears Māori claims against the Crown, concluded that the chiefs who signed the Māori text of the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi did not give up their sovereignty to Britain, which leaves open how and when the Crown gained the sovereignty it now holds.
kingitanga.mechanism: A people can form its own authority in opposition to a colonial state. Force and confiscation can take its land while the movement itself carries on.
kingitanga.founder: Māori chiefs of the central North Island; first king Pōtatau Te Wherowhero
kingitanga.challenge: British invasion of Waikato, July 1863; 486,500 hectares confiscated
kingitanga.recognition: Monarch not recognised in New Zealand law or by many tribes

add_sources.t: The new monarch: Who is Kuīni Nga Wai Hono i te Po?, 1News

mcgirt-v-oklahoma.story: McGirt v. Oklahoma is a 2020 ruling by the United States Supreme Court about who can prosecute crimes on much of eastern Oklahoma. In the 19th century Congress set aside land for the Muscogee (Creek) Nation as a reservation. The question was whether that reservation had ever legally ended when Oklahoma became a state. In a 5 to 4 decision written by Justice Neil Gorsuch, the court held that Congress had never ended it, so the land is still Indian country, the legal term for land under tribal and federal authority. Because of the Major Crimes Act, a federal law, that meant Oklahoma could not prosecute Native Americans for the serious crimes listed in the Act when committed there. Oklahoma's Court of Criminal Appeals then applied the same reasoning to nine other Indigenous nations, so almost all of eastern Oklahoma counts as Indian country. Such cases go to tribal and federal courts. Courts at first threw out past convictions, but less than a year later the state appeals court ruled that McGirt did not apply to old cases. In 2022, in Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, the Supreme Court held that state courts share power over crimes by non-Indians against Indian victims there. The ruling changed who may prosecute crimes on this land and did not make the nations independent states.
mcgirt-v-oklahoma.mechanism: A reservation set up by Congress lasts until Congress ends it. Later court rulings can still narrow what that means in practice.
mcgirt-v-oklahoma.laws: Tribal and federal courts handle major crimes under the Major Crimes Act

nunavut.story: Nunavut is Canada's largest territory, covering 2,093,190 square kilometres of the Arctic, created after the Inuit, the Indigenous people of the region, negotiated a land claim with the Canadian government. Inuit organisations and the federal government began discussing a split of the Northwest Territories in 1976. In a vote across the Northwest Territories on 14 April 1982, most residents backed division. The land-claims agreement was completed in September 1992, and nearly 85 percent of voters ratified it. On 9 July 1993 Parliament passed the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement Act and the Nunavut Act, and the new territory began on 1 April 1999, with Iqaluit as its capital. In 2021 it had 36,858 people, of whom 84 percent were Inuit, and an estimated 43,091 in late 2026. Its assembly is elected without political parties and chooses a premier from among its members, and a council of elders advises on using Inuit knowledge in government. A 2024 agreement gives the territorial government control over its land and resources. Nunavut remains a territory of Canada and makes no claim to be a state.
nunavut.mechanism: A people can gain a territory and a large say in its government through negotiated law while staying inside the country.
nunavut.why: Old text said the Act gave the territory to the Inuit for self-government; Nunavut has a public territorial government with an Inuit majority, so this was reworded. Added 2024 devolution.
nunavut.founder: Inuit organisations and the government of Canada

sami-parliaments.story: The Sámi are an Indigenous people of northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, and they elect their own parliaments in three of those countries. Norway's opened on 9 October 1989 in Karasjok, with 39 members from seven voting districts. Sweden's opened on 26 August 1993 in Kiruna, with 31 members, and its actions must follow decisions of the Riksdag, Sweden's national parliament. Finland's opened on 2 March 1996 in Inari, with 21 members, replacing an earlier elected Sámi delegation. All three hold elections every four years. In Russia a Kola Sámi Assembly was set up on 12 December 2010 in Murmansk, but as of 2017 the authorities did not recognise it as a lawmaking body. The parliaments work together through a Sámi Parliamentary Council, and a Conference of Sámi Parliamentarians has met every three years since 2005. All of these bodies operate inside existing countries, and none claims independence.
sami-parliaments.mechanism: An Indigenous people can elect its own parliaments across several countries, while each body remains under the law of the country where it sits.
sami-parliaments.laws: Sweden's body must follow decisions of the national parliament

ada-kaleh.story: Ada Kaleh was an inhabited island about 1.75 kilometres long in the River Danube, just downstream of Orșova, on what is now the border of Romania and Serbia. Austria and the Ottoman Empire, the Turkish-ruled state, fought over its fortress for a century. When peace was negotiated at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, the delegates forgot about it. The Ottomans lost the land on both banks, but the island stayed Ottoman in law, with Austria-Hungary on one side of the river and Serbia on the other. The Ottoman government kept sending an administrator and a judge. Because of this position, residents paid no tax or customs, were not drafted into the army, and voted in the Ottoman elections of 1908. The island became known as a free port and a smugglers' nest, and it made Turkish delight and rose oil. Austria-Hungary declared sovereignty over it in 1913, Romania occupied it in 1919, and the Treaty of Lausanne made it Romanian in 1923. The remaining Turkish residents had left by 1967. In 1970 the Iron Gates hydroelectric dam flooded the island, and it now lies under water.
ada-kaleh.mechanism: A river island left out of a peace treaty stayed with its old ruler for 45 years, surrounded by other countries and free of their taxes. A later treaty gave it to Romania.
ada-kaleh.founder: Overlooked at the 1878 Congress of Berlin
ada-kaleh.stopped_by: Treaty of Lausanne, 1923, then flooded by the Iron Gates dam in 1970

caspian-convention-2018.story: The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea is a treaty among the five countries around the Caspian, a huge body of salt water of 389,000 square kilometres between Europe and Asia. For decades they argued over whether it counts as a sea or a lake, because the law of the sea applies only to seas. Under an old treaty between Iran and the Soviet Union it was treated as a lake split into two sectors, with fish shared. When the Soviet Union ended, Russia, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Turkmenistan replaced it on the northern shores. Russia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan made deals with each other using median lines, lines halfway between shores. Iran wanted one deal among all five and aimed for a one-fifth share. Iranian patrol boats at times fired on vessels Azerbaijan sent to explore disputed oil fields. After talks running from about 1990, the five leaders signed the convention at Aktau, Kazakhstan, on 12 August 2018. It gives each country 15 nautical miles (about 28 km) of territorial water, which it fully controls, and 10 nautical miles (about 19 km) more of exclusive fishing. The rest of the surface is common space open to the five. The seabed, which holds the oil and gas, is left to deals between countries. The convention takes effect only when all five ratify it, meaning approve it formally. Four have. Iran's cabinet approved it on 22 July 2026 and sent it to parliament, which had not ratified it as of September 2026.
caspian-convention-2018.mechanism: The convention, signed but not yet in force, treats the Caspian as neither fully a sea nor a lake. Its open middle is shared by five named countries, so an outsider has none of the freedoms found on the open ocean.
caspian-convention-2018.recognition: Signed by all five shore countries; ratified by four; not in force as of September 2026

kasikili-sedudu-icj.story: Sedudu, called Kasikili in Namibia, is an island of about 5 square kilometres in the Chobe River on the border between Botswana and Namibia in southern Africa. No one lives there permanently, and floods cover it for several months a year from about March. The dispute came from an 1890 treaty between Germany and Britain, the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty, which settled their colonies in what are now Namibia and Botswana. The treaty put the line in the "main channel" of the river without saying which channel that was. In 1996 the two countries agreed to ask the International Court of Justice, the United Nations court for disputes between countries, to decide the boundary and the island's status. The court studied the river and held in 1999 that the northern channel was the main one. The border therefore follows the thalweg, the deepest line of the channel, north of the island, which places Sedudu in Botswana. The island is now one of the main tourist attractions in the Chobe area.
kasikili-sedudu-icj.mechanism: When a colonial treaty names a river channel as the border, a court can settle who holds an island by deciding which channel the treaty meant, then following its deepest line.
kasikili-sedudu-icj.founder: Botswana and Namibia, by agreement to go to court

lake-constance-no-border.story: Lake Constance is a large lake in central Europe where Germany, Switzerland and Austria meet, and no treaty says where the borders run across most of it. Its shores belong to the German states of Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria, the Swiss cantons of St. Gallen, Thurgau and Schaffhausen, and the Austrian state of Vorarlberg. Areas less than 25 metres deep are treated as belonging to the nearest country. Beyond that depth, no legally binding agreement exists. Switzerland holds that the line goes down the middle of the lake. Austria says the deep part belongs to all the shore states together, an arrangement known as a condominium, meaning shared rule. Germany has kept its opinion ambiguous. Because the three cannot agree, shipping and fishing are handled by separate treaties, so daily life on the water goes on without a line. Under each of the three views the deep water still belongs to one or more of the shore countries, so no one else can claim it, and the question remains unsettled.
lake-constance-no-border.mechanism: A missing border between neighbours is a dispute among them alone. The water still belongs to one or more of the shore countries under every view they hold, so an outsider gains no claim.
lake-constance-no-border.recognition: Three countries hold three different views

migingo-island.story: Migingo is a rock of about 2,000 square metres in Lake Victoria in East Africa, claimed by both Kenya and Uganda and valued for the Nile perch, a large food fish, in the waters around it. Two Kenyan fishermen say they settled it in 1991, and a Ugandan fisherman says he arrived in 2004. Kenya says Ugandan marine police pitched a tent and raised a flag there in June 2004. In February 2009 Kenyans living on the rock were told to buy special Ugandan permits, which set off a diplomatic row. By then it held homes of corrugated metal, four pubs, a pharmacy and an open-air casino. On 13 March 2009 ministers met in Kampala and agreed that Uganda would withdraw its 48 police officers, but a visit two weeks later ended in insults because the police had stayed. Uganda proposed a survey using a 1926 colonial order, copied into its constitution, which draws the border between named islands. In May, President Yoweri Museveni of Uganda conceded the island was Kenyan. A joint survey began on 2 June. Sources differ on what came next. Wikipedia says the results in late July placed Migingo 510 metres inside Kenya and that Uganda lowered its flag and withdrew. A Kenya News Agency report in January 2025 says the joint work stopped in early July when surveyors disagreed, that the Kenyan team later reached the 510-metre figure, and that the report was still unpublished. In August 2025 Kenyan fishermen said Ugandan security officials were still seizing their gear.
migingo-island.mechanism: An old colonial line copied into a constitution places the island in Kenya, and settling there first or raising a flag did not change that. Ugandan officers still act on the water around it, so the dispute continues.
migingo-island.founder: Ugandan marine police raised a flag; Kenyan and Ugandan fishermen settled earlier
migingo-island.pop: 131 reported in 2009; Ugandan police estimated about 500
migingo-island.challenge: A survey reportedly placed it in Kenya but remained unpublished as of January 2025; disputes over waters and policing continue
migingo-island.recognition: Kenyan, according to the 2009 survey and President Museveni

pheasant-island.story: Pheasant Island is a small uninhabited island in the Bidasoa river, between Irun in Spain and Hendaye in France, that the two countries take turns governing. In 1659 it hosted 24 meetings between Spain's minister Luis Méndez de Haro and France's Cardinal Mazarin, and these ended in the Treaty of the Pyrenees. Under that treaty the island is a condominium, meaning two countries share sovereignty over it. The naval commander at Hondarribia in Spain governs it from 1 February to 31 July, and a French official with the title "viceroy of Pheasant Island" governs it from 1 August to 31 January. In practice the mayors of Irun and Hendaye look after it. In January 2018 it measured about 200 metres by 40 metres and was eroding. Nobody lives there and access is forbidden, apart from rare heritage open days. Municipal staff land every six months to clean and garden, and naval personnel from San Sebastián and Bayonne check it every five days. The arrangement has lasted for more than three centuries and still operates.
pheasant-island.mechanism: A treaty can give a river island to two countries at once. Officials of both then have the right to remove anyone who lands there, so no one else can claim it.
pheasant-island.founder: France and Spain, by the Treaty of the Pyrenees
pheasant-island.recognition: Shared by France and Spain as a condominium

santa-rosa-island-amazon.story: Santa Rosa is an island in the Amazon River at the point where Brazil, Colombia and Peru meet, across the water from Leticia in Colombia and Tabatinga in Brazil. About 3,000 people live there, under Peruvian administration going back decades. In June 2025 Peru's Congress made the island a district of its Loreto region. On 5 August 2025 Colombian President Gustavo Petro said Peru had "appropriated it by law", and he warned that the change could cut Leticia, a town of nearly 60,000 people, off from the river. Peru relies on treaties from 1922 and 1929 and treats the island as an extension of Chinería Island. Colombia answers that Santa Rosa had not yet formed when those treaties were signed, so they cannot have assigned it. It also argues that the border follows the deepest line of the Amazon and that new islands have formed on its side. Colombia's foreign ministry says the two countries need to work together on deciding who holds each island. The island remains under Peruvian administration and disputed by Colombia, and the riverbanks there keep shifting.
santa-rosa-island-amazon.mechanism: When a river creates new land after a border treaty, the treaty may not say who owns it. Neighbouring countries then compete for it through their own laws and diplomatic protests.
santa-rosa-island-amazon.recognition: Run by Peru; disputed by Colombia

abaco.story: The Abaco Independence Movement tried to split the Abaco Islands, an inhabited chain in the northern Bahamas, away from the Bahamas as the country became independent from Britain in 1973. Some white residents objected to living under black rule. Chuck Hall and Bert Williams founded the movement in mid-1973 (sources differ between June and August). Its money came from Michael Oliver, a real-estate millionaire based in the United States, whose Phoenix Foundation backed libertarian attempts to create new states, including a platform on the Minerva reefs in the South Pacific in 1972. The movement proposed placing all Crown land in a trust, giving each citizen a one-acre lot and a share of land revenue, and creating a 60-square-mile free trade zone, where goods move without customs duties. Its first convention, on 23 February 1974, was addressed by John Hospers, the 1972 presidential candidate of the American Libertarian Party, who was later refused entry to the Bahamas. In February 1975 Esquire magazine reported that a rising was being planned, and the American arms dealer Mitchell WerBell said Abaco would declare independence on its own. No arrests followed, but the WerBell connection damaged the group. In March 1975 it renamed itself the Abaco Home Rule Movement, denied any military aims and published a draft constitution. The 1977 general election, won by the governing party, effectively ended it, and its newspaper stopped that year. Abaco remains part of the Bahamas.
abaco.mechanism: Foreign libertarian money tried to detach an inhabited territory at the moment a new country was forming. It lost credibility and faded after a national election, with no fighting and no court case.
abaco.founder: Chuck Hall and Bert Williams, funded by Michael Oliver's Phoenix Foundation
abaco.stopped_by: Lost credibility after links to arms dealer Mitchell WerBell; effectively ended by the 1977 election
abaco.challenge: No armed conflict; no one was arrested or charged over a rising

aerican-empire.story: The Aerican Empire is a joke monarchy founded in Canada on 8 May 1987 by Eric Lis, then a child, and a group of friends. It is a micronation, a tiny self-declared country that no government recognises. Its name plays on "American Empire", and its founders say it began as humour. For its first ten years it was almost wholly fictional, claiming a galaxy of invented planets and fighting wars with other micronations that never involved physical contact. It went online in 1997, and in 2000 The New York Times called its site one of the more imaginative micronation sites. It issued novelty passports from 2007, and one was shown that year at an art exhibition at the Palais de Tokyo in Paris. Its first stamps came in 2015. Its flag resembles Canada's, with a yellow smiling face in place of the red maple leaf. Its mission statement says the Empire exists to help bring about a society in which the Empire is no longer needed. Lis remains Emperor, and in 2025 it hosted MicroCon in Montreal, attended by 120 people from 48 micronations.
aerican-empire.mechanism: A micronation whose claim is openly fictional poses no challenge to any government, so no one has a reason to stop it.

aeterna-lucia.name: Sovereign State of Aeterna Lucina
aeterna-lucia.story: The Sovereign State of Aeterna Lucina, also called the Sovereign Humanitarian Mission State of Aeterna Lucina, was a self-declared country on private land in New South Wales, Australia. Paul Neuman, a German migrant who legally changed his name to Paul Baron Neuman and called himself the Supreme Lord, founded it in Byron Bay in 1978. He said Hassan III, the exiled former king of Afghanistan, had made him Baron Neuman of Kara Bagh, and he claimed hundreds of other honours and degrees. He moved the state twice, to Curl Curl in Sydney and then to Cooma, and he sold at least one knighthood, reportedly for 1,900 Australian dollars. In 1990 he was charged with fraud over land sales worth 144,000 Australian dollars, and the case was dropped in 1992. The state lasted until his death, and sources give 1996 as its end.
aeterna-lucia.mechanism: Declaring private land a country and holding a foreign title gave no standing in Australian law. The founder still faced ordinary fraud charges in a state court.
aeterna-lucia.challenge: 1990 fraud charge over land sales, dropped in 1992
aeterna-lucia.why: Name corrected from Aeterna Lucia to Aeterna Lucina per the dedicated Wikipedia article; founder named.

add_sources.t: Sovereign State of Aeterna Lucina, Wikipedia

aigues-mortes.story: The Principality of Aigues-Mortes is a humorous mock state in the walled town of Aigues-Mortes in southern France, started on 21 June 2010 as a parody of Monaco to attract media attention and tourists. Its founders invented a story based on the town's real history. King Louis IX sailed from Aigues-Mortes on two crusades and died in Tunis in 1270. According to the invented tale, on his deathbed he made his loyal squire, Pierrot Pitchoun, Prince of Aigues-Mortes. The current prince is styled Sovereign-Prince Jean-Pierre IV, said to be the 22nd in this line. The group is registered in France as an organisation called LOUPAM. With local merchants and the town's tourist office, it runs an exchange for a local currency, the flamant, and it has taken part in micronation conferences, hosting one in 2016. No government recognises it, and the town remains part of France.
aigues-mortes.mechanism: A local association can call its town a principality as a tourism stunt. French law and government go on working there as before.
aigues-mortes.why: Founder corrected: the list said the city named itself a principality, but the dedicated article says the micronation is a registered association (LOUPAM), working with merchants and the tourist office.

akhzivland.story: Achzivland was a one-family micronation, a tiny self-declared country, on the northern coast of Israel near the Lebanese border. Eli Avivi came across the old site of Achziv in 1952 and settled among its buildings, selling fish to a nearby kibbutz, a collective farm. He later married Rina. In the 1960s the state decided to turn the area into a national park and sent bulldozers. Rina told the BBC that the army let him stay on condition that he worked as an undercover agent for Shin Bet, Israel's domestic intelligence agency. When authorities put up a fence that blocked the couple's way to the sea, they tore up their passports in protest and declared independence in 1971. Achzivland had its own passport, which asked that bearers be allowed to pass freely, and it drew hippies and celebrities, including Sophia Loren. Israel never recognised the place, though a court leased the land to Avivi for 99 years and a judge ruled that creating a country without permission was not an offence. In 2015 Avivi, then 85 and frail, told the BBC that the state did everything it could to get him out. He died in May 2018, aged 88, leaving Rina as the only other citizen. Ynet reported in January 2026 that she was still the site's one permanent resident.
akhzivland.mechanism: A long-tolerated occupant can outlast a state's plans in a personal stand-off and even win a lease. The lease is an ordinary contract under Israeli law and gives no sovereignty.
akhzivland.challenge: Survived several attempts to remove him

aramoana.story: The Independent State of Aramoana was a protest against an aluminium smelter in New Zealand. Aramoana is a small settlement on a sand spit at the mouth of Otago Harbour, near Dunedin on the South Island.
