The smelter was first proposed in 1974, and by the late 1970s a group of companies, Fletcher Challenge, CSR of Australia and Alusuisse of Switzerland, wanted to build it there. Prime Minister Robert Muldoon's government backed it as a project of national importance. Opponents wanted to protect a wetland, the community and Māori burial sites. Through the Save Aramoana Campaign, residents declared independence on 23 December 1980. They produced flags, passports, stamps and a mock tax form to sell for money, ran a travelling embassy, and set up a mock border post on the access road. In April 1981 the government confirmed residents would be evicted the following year, but Alusuisse then left the group. The government kept saying the project would continue, but nothing happened, and the later Labour government did not support it. The smelter was not built, Aramoana returned to being an ordinary part of New Zealand, and the nearby mudflats are now a wildlife sanctuary.
aramoana.mechanism: A mock declaration of independence has no legal effect, but the publicity and money it raises can help a local campaign against a government project.
aramoana.founder: Aramoana residents, through the Save Aramoana Campaign
aramoana.passports: Protest passports sold to raise money
aramoana.stopped_by: Ended once the smelter plan collapsed

atlantium.story: The Empire of Atlantium is a micronation, a self-declared country that no government recognises, founded in Sydney, Australia, by three teenagers on 27 November 1981. George Cruickshank became head of state as Emperor George II. The group went inactive around 1990 and revived in 1999. Its capital moved from a 10-square-metre plot in the Sydney suburb of Narwee to a 61-square-metre apartment in Potts Point, and on 12 January 2008 to the Province of Aurora, 0.76 square kilometres of land about 350 km southwest of Sydney. Almost 3,000 citizens were on its rolls in 2015, from over 100 countries. Most signed up online and never visited. It sold coins, stamps and banknotes in a currency called the imperial solidus, and it appointed unofficial representatives in about ten countries. Most of its activity is not tied to any land. Both of its properties stay under Australian law, and no country recognises it.
atlantium.mechanism: Buying land gave the group a base, but the land stayed under Australian law. Owning property does not make it a country.

austenasia.founder: Jonathan Austen and his father Terry Austen
austenasia.story: The Empire of Austenasia is a micronation, a tiny self-declared country, based in a house in the London Borough of Sutton in England. Jonathan Austen, a teenage student, and his father Terry founded it on 20 September 2008 by sending a declaration of independence for their house in Carshalton to their local Member of Parliament, Tom Brake. Terry became Emperor and Jonathan Prime Minister. It claims to succeed the Roman Empire and has adopted Roman touches such as consuls and a senate. It has grown as new citizens declared their own properties part of it, including houses in Britain, a holiday home in the Hebrides, part of a university campus in Australia, and places in the United States, Turkey and India. In May 2011 Jonathan met Brake, who asked Foreign Secretary William Hague what criteria Britain uses to recognise new states. After several other emperors, Jonathan took the throne in 2013. Jonathan stepped back in April 2024 and handed the running of it to a Prince Regent, Aggelos I. No report says any government recognises it.
austenasia.mechanism: When property owners declare their homes part of a micronation, no border moves and the law on those plots stays the same.

avram.story: The Grand Duchy of Avram is a micronation in Tasmania, Australia, that claims no land and works mainly as a private bank issuing its own money. John Charlton Rudge, a former Liberal Party member of the Tasmanian parliament, started it in the early 1980s and calls it "philosophical, not territorial". He styles himself Grand Duke and claims dozens of titles. His Royal Bank of Avram opened in shops he owned in George Town and later moved to Strahan. Customers exchanged Australian dollars for its banknotes and coins, which were linked to the value of gold. Because the bank had no licence, the Australian government seized Rudge's currency reserves and went to the Federal Court. According to Wikipedia, six cases followed at a cost of about 22 million Australian dollars, the courts found he had done nothing illegal, and they ordered the property returned. Rudge resumed banking and issued more coins and notes, the most recent dated 2008. No later report describes the bank's activity.
avram.mechanism: A bank with no territory is judged under ordinary banking and criminal law. Here the courts found no crime, but that gave the duchy no standing as a state.
avram.currency: Own banknotes and coins, the Avram and Ducal
avram.challenge: Six court cases; courts found no illegal activity

bunte-republik-neustadt.founder: Gregor Kunz and friends in Dresden's Neustadt district
bunte-republik-neustadt.story: The Bunte Republik Neustadt, German for Colourful Republic of Neustadt, was a mock state in the Äußere Neustadt district of Dresden, in eastern Germany. It was proclaimed for a neighbourhood festival on 22 to 24 June 1990. Gregor Kunz, who became its first monarch, said the idea came up in conversation at a local pub and was put together within two or three months. A provisional government formed, led by a "monarch without portfolio" and ministers with humorous titles, and it demanded annexation by the Vatican. A white line painted on the streets marked its borders, around one block of the district. It created a currency, the Neustadtmark, with set rates against the East and West German marks, and a flag with a Mickey Mouse head in a wreath of wheat, modelled on the East German coat of arms. In 1993 the government dissolved itself by "going bathing" in the River Elbe, a joke about its pollution. The state ended there, but the festival continues each June, much less political, with no single organiser since 2002.
bunte-republik-neustadt.mechanism: A street festival can use the forms of a state for satire. It had no legal effect, and German law applied throughout.

capitol-hill-occupied-protest.story: The Capitol Hill Occupied Protest, also called the Capitol Hill Organized Protest, CHOP or CHAZ, was a protest zone in the Capitol Hill neighbourhood of Seattle, Washington, in June 2020. In May a police officer in Minneapolis murdered George Floyd, and protests spread across the country. In Seattle, protesters and riot police clashed near the police department's East Precinct building from 1 June. Mayor Jenny Durkan's office told police to remove barricades, and on 8 June police boarded up and left the building. Who gave that order is disputed. Protesters then declared the area around it an autonomous zone, meaning one run by themselves, covering two intersections at the corners of Cal Anderson Park and the roads leading up to them. It had no official leaders and met in daily assemblies, with free food, film screenings, medical stations and gardens. Its main demands were a 50 percent cut to police funding and no criminal charges for protesters. Accounts varied from a block party to reports of intimidation by local businesses and residents. Shootings on 20, 21, 23 and 29 June killed two people and wounded others. After the last one, Durkan declared the gathering unlawful, and on 1 July police cleared it, after 23 days, arresting dozens. The zone made no claim to be a country and sought no recognition. Lawsuits followed, and the city later paid settlements including $10 million to protesters and $3.65 million to affected businesses.
capitol-hill-occupied-protest.mechanism: Declaring a city district self-run has no legal effect. It lasts only as long as the city government chooses not to send police.
capitol-hill-occupied-protest.founder: Protesters after the murder of George Floyd

conch-republic.story: The Conch Republic is a joke country declared by the city of Key West, Florida, in protest against a federal roadblock. In April 1982 the United States Border Patrol set up a roadblock and checkpoint in the Florida Keys, which held up residents and tourists. Key West's city council complained to the federal government and got no answer, and an attempt to win a court order against the roadblock failed. So on 23 April 1982 Mayor Dennis Wardlow and the council declared Key West independent, with Wardlow as prime minister. The new republic declared war on the United States by breaking a stale Cuban loaf over the head of a man in a naval uniform, surrendered to him after one minute, and applied for one billion dollars in foreign aid. The event has been repeated every 23 April since then as a week-long festival, and the name now covers all the Keys. Representatives were invited to the 1994 Summit of the Americas in Miami and the 1995 Florida Jubilee. The organisation calls itself a sovereign state of mind and works mainly as a tourism promoter.
conch-republic.mechanism: A mock secession can bring publicity to a real complaint after a court case fails. It changes nothing about the place's legal status.
conch-republic.pop: Key West residents; it has no population as a state
conch-republic.laws: Tourist festival with a secretary general
conch-republic.challenge: A court order against the roadblock failed before the declaration; no one challenged the joke
conch-republic.recognition: None; officials were invited to some events
conch-republic.cost: Applied for $1 billion in foreign aid as a joke

coral-sea-kingdom.story: The Gay and Lesbian Kingdom of the Coral Sea Islands was a protest state on the Coral Sea Islands, small uninhabited islands and reefs east of the Great Barrier Reef that belong to Australia. In May 2004 the Australian government brought a bill to Parliament defining marriage as between a man and a woman. In response, on 14 June 2004 activists led by Dale Parker Anderson raised the rainbow flag on Cato Island, the territory's highest point, and claimed the islands as a homeland for gay and lesbian people. A plaque there records the date, and a campsite called Heaven was named the capital. In a scheme modelled on Israel's Law of Return, which lets Jews settle in Israel, any gay or lesbian person could gain residence and citizenship. Anderson was elected administrator and then declared emperor. The scholar Judy Lattas of Macquarie University, who interviewed him in 2007, treats it as a real secession and argues that gay nationalism may need territorial claims to secure rights. Wikipedia calls it a symbolic protest. Its leaders dissolved the kingdom on 17 November 2017, after the Yes result in Australia's postal survey on same-sex marriage.
coral-sea-kingdom.mechanism: This claim on undisputed Australian territory was a form of protest. It borrowed the idea of secession to press for equal marriage law, and its leaders ended it once that campaign succeeded.
coral-sea-kingdom.pop: No one lived there; a campsite was the claimed capital
coral-sea-kingdom.laws: Anderson elected administrator and declared emperor; anthem "I Am What I Am"
coral-sea-kingdom.challenge: No state challenge is reported; the islands stayed Australian

crypto-valley-zug.story: Crypto Valley is a nickname for Zug, a Swiss town of 30,934 people at the end of 2020 and capital of the canton (state) of Zug, because of the many cryptocurrency companies based there. They include Ethereum, Cardano, Polkadot and Bitcoin Suisse. Zug has long drawn companies with low taxes, and it is close to Zürich. In 2016 the town began accepting digital currency for small fees up to 200 francs, converting it into Swiss francs straight away to reduce the risk of price swings. A Crypto Valley Association had formed by 2018, with Oliver Bussmann as president. The German newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported in 2021 that taxes in the canton could be paid in Bitcoin. Zug remains an ordinary part of Switzerland, under Swiss law.
crypto-valley-zug.mechanism: A local government can adopt new technology and attract businesses inside national law. Doing so gives it no separate legal status.

edge-esmeralda.story: Edge Esmeralda is a month-long temporary village in Healdsburg, California, about an hour north of San Francisco, where people test new ways of living together. It is organised by a team called Edge City and described as a spin-off of Zuzalu, a similar gathering started by Vitalik Buterin of the cryptocurrency Ethereum. Its 2024 edition drew about 1,300 people, and the P2P Foundation calls it the first openly family-friendly village of this kind. It was held again in 2025. Its backers aim to build a permanent village. The Esmeralda Land Company, associated with the organiser Devon Zuegel, has a concept for 266 acres at the southeast edge of Cloverdale, on an old lumber mill site below an airport approach. In 2026 an airport land use commission paused its review until safety and land-use issues are resolved. The gathering and any village would come under ordinary California and local law.
edge-esmeralda.mechanism: A gathering in a California town stays under normal American law. Any permanent village must pass the same planning and safety reviews as other developments.

add_sources.t: Airport safety design slows proposed Esmeralda settlement, Patch

federal-republic-of-montmartre-ny.story: The Most Serene Federal Republic of Montmartre was a mock country claiming Manhattan's Theater District in New York City, from about 39th to 59th Street. Its founder and president was Barry Alan Richmond, a stage actor and director, who proclaimed it around 1965 and said it dated from a French colony founded in 1636. He called it a "political fiction" and part of what he termed "total theater", and he paid for phone listings in the government pages of the Manhattan directory. New York Telephone wanted the "Montmartre Govt Of" listing removed, and in 1977 the dispute went to the New York Public Service Commission, the state body that regulates utilities. An examiner ruled for the company on 30 June, and the commission set that ruling aside on 7 July. The company still printed 955,000 directories without the listing that August, and Richmond lost a court case to restore it in April 1978. In December 1979 he announced that the commission had ruled for him. A 2001 article found him still running it, claiming half of Kennedy Airport. No later report describes it.
federal-republic-of-montmartre-ny.mechanism: The nearest this project came to official notice was a dispute over phone listings before a state regulator, which decided a question of telephone rules and nothing about statehood.
federal-republic-of-montmartre-ny.challenge: Phone book dispute before New York's utility regulator and courts, 1977 to 1979

Drama Unfolds of a Little Empire, Boy Reporter

fordlandia.story: Fordlândia was a company town that the American carmaker Henry Ford built in the Amazon rainforest, on the Tapajós river in the state of Pará, Brazil. He started it in 1928 to grow rubber for his cars, on a land concession of about 10,000 square kilometres, meaning land the government let him use under agreed terms. Ford was exempted from taxes on goods exported from Brazil in exchange for 9 percent of profits, 7 percent for the national government and 2 percent for local towns. The rubber trees were planted close together, which made them easy prey for disease and insects. In 1930 workers revolted in the cafeteria over the food, cut telegraph wires and drove out managers until the Brazilian Army arrived and ended it. Ford Motor Company gave up on the town in 1934 and moved upriver to Belterra. In 1945 Henry Ford II sold the land to the Brazilian government at a loss of over $20 million. About 90 residents remained until the 2000s, and about 3,000 people lived there by 2017.
fordlandia.mechanism: A company can run a town on land granted by a government, but the country's army and law still apply there. When workers revolted in 1930, Brazil's army ended it.
fordlandia.stopped_by: Ford gave up the town in 1934 and sold the land in 1945
fordlandia.laws: Brazilian law; export-tax exemption in exchange for 9 percent of profits
fordlandia.challenge: Workers' revolt in 1930, ended by the Brazilian Army
fordlandia.recognition: None sought; a land concession from Brazil
fordlandia.cost: Sold in 1945 at a loss of over $20 million

forvik.story: Forvik was a state declared by one man on Forewick Holm, a one-hectare islet in the Shetland Islands, north of mainland Scotland. Stuart Hill, from Essex in England, was shipwrecked there in 2001 during a failed trip around Britain, and he was nicknamed Captain Calamity. He settled in Shetland and argued that the islands were never formally handed to Scotland or Britain, so British rule there had no legal basis. On 21 June 2008 he declared the islet the Sovereign State of Forvik, a dependency of the British Crown outside the United Kingdom and the European Union. In 2010 he helped launch a Sovereign Nation of Shetland. In 2011, aged 68, he was charged with 12 motoring offences, including having no insurance, tax, licence or vehicle safety certificate, on vans he said were consular vehicles for Forvik. At Lerwick Sheriff Court (a sheriff is a Scottish judge) he was locked up for 20 minutes after refusing to answer the charges. He then presented a 71-page argument that the court had no power in Shetland. Sheriff Graeme Napier heard it over two days, called Hill deluded and seriously misguided, and dismissed it. In December 2011 Hill was found guilty on six charges, fined £1,400, and given 100 hours of unpaid work and a six-month driving ban. He kept campaigning, and in December 2025, aged 82, he was again found guilty of driving offences after another sheriff rejected the same argument.
forvik.mechanism: A Scottish court held that historical arguments about how Shetland passed to Scotland do not free anyone from the jurisdiction of the courts, meaning their power to decide a case, or from ordinary driving law.
forvik.stopped_by: Lerwick Sheriff Court rejected his argument and convicted him in 2011
forvik.pop: No one lives on the islet
forvik.laws: Declared a dependency of the British Crown
forvik.challenge: Lost: a sheriff rejected his 71-page challenge to Scottish courts' power

free-republic-of-wendland.story: The Free Republic of Wendland was a protest camp near Gorleben in northern West Germany, set up to stop a planned nuclear waste site. Gorleben was being studied as a place to store radioactive waste underground, and on 3 May 1980 anti-nuclear activists occupied one of its test drilling sites, number 1004, and proclaimed a republic. About 5,000 people took part, and around 1,000 stayed permanently. They built about 110 huts of wood and clay, a Friendship House, greenhouses, an infirmary and a sauna. Their information centre sold a passport called the Wendenpass for 10 marks, said to be valid for the entire universe so long as its owner could still laugh. Radio Free Wendland began pirate broadcasts, unlicensed radio, on 18 May. The state interior minister called the proclamation high treason. On 4 June, on Chancellor Helmut Schmidt's orders, about 3,500 police and border guards cleared the camp, while about 2,000 occupiers held a largely peaceful sit-in. The republic ended that day. A 30th anniversary gathering in 2010 drew about 800 people.
free-republic-of-wendland.mechanism: Occupying a site chosen by the state and calling it a republic brought a police clearance after a month. A minister called it treason, but the declaration had no legal effect.
free-republic-of-wendland.stopped_by: Police and federal border guards, 4 June 1980

frestonia.story: Frestonia was a mock independent state set up by squatters on Freston Road in west London to stop their homes being demolished. The street held rows of condemned Victorian cottages, which squatters had moved into from 1974. When the Greater London Council, the city's government, planned to clear the 1.8-acre site, the 120 residents all took the surname Bramley so the council would have to rehouse them together. The council then threatened eviction. At a public meeting of 200 people, resident Nicholas Albery suggested seceding, inspired by the film Passport to Pimlico and a visit to Christiania in Copenhagen. A referendum showed 94 percent in favour. They declared independence on 31 October 1977, applied to the United Nations and warned that peacekeeping troops might be needed. The actor David Rappaport became foreign minister, the playwright Heathcote Williams ambassador to Britain, and a two-year-old child education minister. They issued stamps and visas. Shadow Chancellor Geoffrey Howe sent a supportive letter, and Williams won a court ruling that, for a dispute over his play The Immortalist, the area was not part of the United Kingdom. The press coverage made demolition harder, and by 1982 the council had dropped it. There were then 23 houses and 97 residents, who formed a housing co-operative and negotiated with the Notting Hill Housing Trust, a housing charity. The co-operative still manages homes on the site, and the community no longer claims independence.
frestonia.mechanism: Here a mock secession worked as a bargaining tactic. Publicity made demolition harder for the housing authority, and the residents got what they wanted through a co-operative under ordinary law.
frestonia.founder: Squatters of Freston Road; Nicholas Albery proposed independence
frestonia.stopped_by: Ended when residents formed a housing co-op and made a deal with the Notting Hill Housing Trust
frestonia.laws: Referendum, ministers and a Latin motto; applied to the United Nations
frestonia.challenge: Blocked demolition; absorbed through a housing deal

ganienkeh.story: Ganienkeh is a community of traditionalist Mohawks, an Indigenous nation, near Altona in northern New York State, whose residents call it an independent North American Indian state. In May 1974 a group occupied Moss Lake, a girls' camp near Old Forge, New York, claiming it as historic Mohawk land and sending a manifesto to the United Nations and President Nixon. The armed occupation ended in 1977 after nearly 200 negotiating sessions, when the group agreed to move to land at Miner Lake, leased through a body called the Turtle Island Trust. The state's top court upheld the lease in 1981, and it has run month to month since 1992. Relations with New York have never been defined. In 1990 a rifle shot traced to the area wounded a doctor on a Vermont National Guard helicopter, and an 11-day armed standoff followed with no arrests. Businesses there include tax-free bingo, cigarettes and an unlicensed casino. Clinton County auctioned 11 of the trust's land parcels in 2012 over about $300,000 in back taxes, and a 2025 ruling favoured the county. The community continues to live there on those terms.
ganienkeh.mechanism: Negotiation with New York State produced a lease and left the question of sovereignty undefined. Courts have since ruled against the trust over back taxes, which shows the state's law still reaches the land.
ganienkeh.laws: Community meetings; alcohol and recreational drugs banned
ganienkeh.challenge: Tax auction of 11 parcels; a final ruling for the county in 2025

glacier-republic.story: The Glacier Republic is a mock state that the environmental group Greenpeace declared over Chile's glaciers on 5 March 2014, to push Chile into passing a law protecting them. Greenpeace objected to mining companies building on or near glaciers. It said Chile's law left a legal vacuum, because neither the constitution nor the water code names glaciers as a public good that must be protected, and Chile had no specific glacier law. It also pointed to unclear points in the border between Chile and Argentina. It took out a full-page advertisement in The New York Times, and more than 40,000 people signed up as citizens within ten days. Greenpeace said the republic would hand the glaciers back to Chile once a suitable law passed. Wikipedia cites Chilean laws that it says already cover glaciers, including the Civil Code, which makes waters state property, and an environmental law listing glaciers among protected wetlands. Six deputies introduced a glacier bill in 2014, and it was still being debated in late 2015. No report says whether a law has since passed.
glacier-republic.mechanism: A campaign group used the language of statehood to press for a national law. The claim has no legal force, and Greenpeace itself says it will end the republic once the law it wants is passed.
